title: Orion above the VLT
caption: Orion and the Milky Way above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The constellation Orion hangs upside down above ESO's Very Large Telescope, as though diving toward the Atacama Desert. It appears head down because the VLT is in the Southern Hemisphere. Below, the four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes point up at the night sky.

The Milky Way, crossed by dark lanes of dust, rises over Melipal, the third Unit Telescope, and the bright star Capella glints just above it. Up and to the left, Orion's belt and sword, which holds the Orion Nebula, sit between blue Rigel and orange Betelgeuse.

The picture is packed with other sights. The red Rosette Nebula glows in the middle part of the Milky Way, and Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, hangs over the whole scene. Just above Unit Telescope 2, Kueyen, a red patch marks the California Nebula, with the blue Pleiades star cluster a little to its upper left.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The bright stars of Orion are easy to see with the naked eye, but the red glow of the nebulae only shows up clearly in a long camera exposure.

explore: The colours of stars carry information: a blue star such as Rigel is hotter than an orange one such as Betelgeuse. Red nebulae like the Rosette and California glow because of hydrogen gas energised by nearby stars.
alt: The constellation Orion upside down above the Very Large Telescope, with the Milky Way, red nebulae, the blue Pleiades and bright stars in the sky.
